name: Avava
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry. 2006. The Avava language of central Malakula (Vanuatu). Edited by John Lynch. Pacific Linguistics 574. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, The Australian National University. (ANU Open Research repository PDF, handle 1885/146274)
catalog_quote: 2.3 Stress Stress in Avava appears to follow the pattern that is encountered in most of the neighbouring languages, with stress being attracted to the penultimate syllable where the final syllable contains just a single vowel. When a final syllable is closed and it contains a diphthong or a long vowel, that syllable is stressed. For stress assignment purposes, one of the automatically syllabified liquids or nasals also counts as a separate syllable.

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the held ANU Open Research PDF/text of Crowley 2006 at sec. 2.3, pp. 36-37, and it is the only stress passage in the book. Crowley 2006 is the sole descriptive work on Avava in Glottolog 5.1 and nothing newer or instrumental surfaced in the (constrained) web search; the linked Lynch papers are comparative. The classification 'weight-hedged', right edge, heavy = closed final syllable with diphthong/long vowel, syllabic liquids/nasals counting as syllables, faithfully renders Crowley's hedged statement, and the hedge is already carried in the record (qv weight-sensitive (tentative), exq_ 'appears to follow'). no reclassification or re-read is indicated; the only conceivable upgrade is an instrumental check against Crowley's PARADISEC audio, listed at low priority.
